reading.body:
A single Sterling campus, EdgeCore Ashburn AS02, holds 114 MW of IT capacity, which is 7.1 percent of all published data center load in Virginia and third-largest among the 25 state facilities that disclose a megawatt figure.

The disclosure gap is the real story. Virginia has 330 mapped data centers, but only 25 publish capacity, so the state total of 1,603 MW is a floor rather than a measurement. One facility accounting for 7.1 percent of that floor shows how concentrated the disclosed load is, and how much load sits outside the accounting entirely.

For AI this matters because capacity is a power number before it is a chip number. A 114 MW campus is a material block of firm load, and its position in Ashburn places it on the region's existing transmission and network backbone rather than at the edge of it. The accelerator counts sometimes attached to figures like this are arithmetic from an assumed watts-per-rack, not observed hardware, and should be read as an illustration of density rather than an inventory.

What the data does not cover is the constraint that decides whether more of this gets built. There is no interconnection queue position, no generation or supply mix, no utilization, and no indication of how much of Virginia's undisclosed capacity is comparable in size. LEED certification speaks to the building, not to the power behind it.
